summary: This document defines a framework for energy management of devices in or attached to communication networks. It describes a physical reference model and an information model built around Energy Objects, which have identity, classification and context and can be monitored or controlled.

plainLanguage.summary: The EMAN framework gives network equipment a common way to describe its power use and power connections. A management system can use that information to monitor devices and, where supported, change their power states.

questions: how to monitor power in network devices
what is the eman energy management framework
subtitle: A model for monitoring and controlling energy-related information about networked equipment.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a common model for describing equipment, its power use, and the connections between equipment in a power system.
tldr.mechanism: The Energy Management framework represents devices, components, and power interfaces as Energy Objects with identity, context, measurements, controls, and relationships.
tldr.outcome: The framework gives management systems a shared way to represent energy information and the physical power topology, separately from the communications topology.

today: RFC 7326 is an Informational document published in September 2014. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Energy Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 7326 defines an Energy Management (EMAN) framework for devices and components within or connected to communications networks. It follows the requirements in RFC 6988 and covers monitoring power, energy, demand, power attributes, and batteries, as well as controlling power states.

The framework covers devices that use or provide energy, their components, and systems that support energy management. It does not cover non-electrical equipment, energy procurement, or the environmental impact of energy use.
sections.plainLanguage: EMAN describes how a management system can monitor energy use in networked equipment. It can also describe controls for changing a device's power state.

sections.title: Devices, Components, and Power Interfaces
sections.content:
An Energy Object is the framework's basic representation of equipment managed for energy. The model has three kinds: a Device, a Component within a device, and a Power Interface where energy is received or provided.

A power interface is separate from a network interface. It can represent an inlet or outlet, such as a device's power connection or a socket on a power distribution unit. The framework allows a management system to describe equipment even when it is monitored through a gateway rather than directly over IP.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework represents a whole device, a part inside it, or a connection that carries power. These objects describe the power system, which may differ from the network that carries management messages.

sections.title: Information About Energy Objects
sections.content:
Energy Objects can have an identifier, a name, and context such as their role, importance, keywords, or Energy Management Domain. This information helps an energy management system group equipment and interpret its measurements.

Measurement attributes describe power, energy, demand, and electrical properties. Power is a rate of energy transfer; energy is accumulated over time. Values can be actual, estimated, or static, and the framework provides attributes to describe their method and accuracy.
sections.plainLanguage: Each Energy Object can say what it is and where it fits in the organization. Its measurements distinguish power at a point in time from energy accumulated over an interval.

sections.title: Power States and Control
sections.content:
A Power State describes a device's condition, capabilities, power use, and response to input. An Energy Object can support one or more Power State Sets, including sets defined by IEEE 1621, DMTF, or EMAN. The framework includes attributes for a requested state, the actual state, and state statistics.

A device may take time to move into a requested state, so the requested state and current state can differ. An implementation reports the change when it occurs. The framework does not require every device to support every state.
sections.plainLanguage: A power state describes how a device is operating and how much power it uses. A requested change may take time, so the framework distinguishes the requested state from the state the device is actually in.

sections.title: Power, Metering, and Aggregation Relationships
sections.content:
Energy Objects can describe three kinds of relationships. A Power Source Relationship says which object provides power to another. A Metering Relationship says which object measures another. An Aggregation Relationship says which object combines energy-management information from other objects.

These relationships let a management system represent power wiring, measurement coverage, and collected values. The framework notes that an administrator may need to configure relationships when they cannot be discovered automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: Relationships describe who supplies power, who measures it, and who combines measurements. These links help a management system understand the power system even when it cannot discover every connection itself.

sections.title: Protecting Measurements and Controls
sections.content:
Energy information and controls can be sensitive. Reading or changing attributes without proper protection can harm network operations. Implementations need to protect access to measurements and to control operations, including power-state changes.

For SNMP-based implementations, the RFC recommends SNMPv3 security and access controls. It warns that unauthorized changes to power states, device context, or energy history can disrupt equipment or reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: Energy measurements can reveal information, and power controls can disrupt equipment. Protect access so only authorized users can read sensitive data or change settings.
